note: THE SIGN FLIP MEASURED DIRECTLY - the exact question Ruling 1 said makes this one chapter. But NOT identified: cross-country aggregate panel, endogeneity tested for GDP and FLFP only, no instrument for credit. Secondary pool per the scope memo's rule on aggregate designs.

study: Fertility and Financial Development: US Counties in the 19th Century
exposure: presence of a bank in the county
note: FDT-era Arm S estimate. Authors read it as support for the old-age-security motive - which is C.3.c's motive under Wall 1, so the ROUTING of this study needs the PI ruling. Associational: OLS on a county cross-section.

study: Fertility and Financial Development: US Counties in the 19th Century
exposure: presence of a bank in the county
note: Second outcome from the same study; do not treat as an independent estimate.

study: The impact of access to credit and capital markets on fertility: China
estimate: sign only: crowding-out effect of pension increase on fertility WHEN credit constraints bind
note: Interaction claim rather than a level effect: the pension crowd-out operates ONLY where credit constraints bind. If it survives a full read this is the clearest statement of the Arm S / C.3.c interaction in the pool.

study: Rainfall risk, fertility and development: American demographic transition
exposure: rainfall variability INTERACTED WITH access to financial services (banks per county / banks per farm)
estimate: interaction negative in sign but economically small and statistically INSIGNIFICANT
SETTING_FINANCE_DEPTH: banks per county, time-varying; irrigation and machinery also measured
note: THE ARM S ESTIMATE IN THIS PAPER. An UNINFORMATIVE null, not a precise zero: the author writes it is 'hard to say whether financial services could not or were not used for risk coping or whether the available measures of access to financial services are simply too crude'. Record it as imprecise, not as evidence of no effect. NOTE the contrast within the same table: the irrigation and machinery interactions DO attenuate the buffer effect, so risk-mitigating TECHNOLOGY works where the financial-access measure does not.

study: Do credit supply shocks affect fertility choices?
exposure: US banking deregulation of the 1980s (staggered state adoption)
note: THE CHAPTER'S FIRST IDENTIFIED ESTIMATE. Exogenous variation in the TIMING of state banking deregulation. Sign POSITIVE: more credit supply, more fertility - Arm B's predicted direction.

study: Do credit supply shocks affect fertility choices?
exposure: doubling of household credit at state level (Bartik IV on pre-recession bank share)
outcome: propensity to give birth in the next year
estimate: +9.5 pp on a 7.7 pp base (7.7 -> 17.2 pp)
note: Second identified design in the same paper, different shock. A one-SD increase in credit = 0.121 SD increase in the propensity to give birth; a 32% increase in credit = +3.2 pp. Stronger for young women and for families with unemployed husbands.

study: The Babies of Mortgage Market Deregulation (a.k.a. The Babies of Financial Deregulation)
exposure: mortgage market deregulation - a US federal regulator ruling creating geographic heterogeneity in access to mortgage credit
note: SECOND IDENTIFIED ESTIMATE. ONE STUDY IN THREE VERSIONS: 'The Babies of Financial Deregulation' (SSRN 2016), this SSRN working paper (2020) and the RFS article - all Isaac Hacamo, same regulator-ruling design. Do not count more than once. Author's supplemental tests REJECT income and housing-wealth channels and point to ACCESS TO SPACE as the mechanism - which sits on the C.2.c boundary (space is a housing attribute) even though the varying object is credit. Sign POSITIVE, Arm B's direction.

study: Do Mortgage Interest Subsidies Affect Fertility and Housing Purchase Decisions?
exposure: preferential mortgage rates / mortgage interest deduction scheme
estimate: NO effect on fertility (first stage verified: mortgage burden -7.9%, and -17.6% outside the most expensive cities)
source: ABSTRACT (full text on the residual retrieval list)
note: THIRD IDENTIFIED ARM B ESTIMATE AND THE FIRST IDENTIFIED NULL. It is an INFORMATIVE null - the policy demonstrably cut mortgage burden by 7.9%, so the zero on fertility is not a failed first stage. Contrast with the two positive identified estimates: those are credit-SUPPLY/access shocks (extensive margin - can you borrow), this is a COST reduction for people already borrowing (intensive margin). That distinction may be the reconciliation. Numbers are abstract-sourced.

study: Credit Availability, Intergenerational Interactions and Family Fertility Decisions
estimate: INVERTED-U: credit expansion raises fertility up to a point, then lowers it; marginal effect heterogeneous in household structure
source: ABSTRACT (full text on the residual retrieval list)
note: Fixed-effects Poisson + IV on China Family Panel Studies 2018-2022. A WITHIN-SETTING nonlinearity, distinct from the cross-setting sign flip in the aggregate panel - but the same theme: the sign of the credit effect depends on where on the curve a setting sits. Also reports bequests raising fertility INTENTIONS via liquidity and educational investment suppressing fertility via quantity-quality - different OUTCOME_LEVEL, record separately at full text. Numbers are abstract-sourced.

study: Microcredit, Family Planning Programs, and Contraceptive Behavior: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Ethiopia
exposure: randomised allocation of administrative areas to credit+FP / CREDIT ONLY / FP only / control
outcome: number of births in the previous three years
estimate: all estimates negative, magnitude always small, -0.106 to -0.166; some statistically significant
SETTING_FINANCE_DEPTH: rural Ethiopia, low-income; formal finance thin
note: THE CHAPTER'S ONLY RANDOMISED ESTIMATE and the credit arm is SEPARATELY randomised. Context that matters for reading the null: fertility ROSE in the study area over the period - TFR 5.5 to 6.0 births and births in the last 3 years 0.51 to 0.55, both significant - and the authors say the rise in contraceptive use 'does not appear to have had much effect on fertility'. Those are sample-wide time trends, NOT treatment effects; do not confuse them.

study: Microcredit, Family Planning Programs, and Contraceptive Behavior: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Ethiopia
note: OPPOSITE SIGN TO THE REALIZED OUTCOME IN THE SAME EXPERIMENT. Authors: 'consistent with microcredit leading to an increase in the demand for children.' This single study is why OUTCOME_LEVEL is load-bearing for the chapter - a synthesis pooling realized and desired here would average a null against a positive.

study: Do Microfinance Programs Change Fertility? Evidence Using Panel Data from Bangladesh
outcome: recent fertility (birth in the last 5 years)
estimate: coefficient -0.14, t = -1.54, NOT significant (p = 0.17); prospective fertility p = 0.29
note: Negative point estimate, not significant, on both recent and prospective fertility. Context: the sample's own probability of a birth in the last 5 years fell 0.55 to 0.48 between rounds, so a time trend runs alongside. Author's stated conclusion is no significant fertility effect of participation or access.

study: The role of digital financial inclusion in increasing fertility intentions: evidence from China
note: INTENTION outcome, positive - consistent with the desires arm of Desai and Tarozzi and inconsistent with the realized nulls. Instrumented but the instrument is not a policy shock; recorded identified: NO pending a closer read of the first stage.
